lead: A system is judged by four separate questions. Does it obey superposition (linearity)? Does a delayed input give only a delayed output (time invariance)? Does the output at an instant depend only on past and present input (causality)? Does every bounded input give a bounded output (BIBO stability)? Each question has a short definition and is answered with a counterexample when the system fails. These four tests decide whether the LTI tools of convolution and the Laplace transform apply, so they are asked early in every signals and systems exam.
prereq: You need the system operator idea and CT/DT notation from Chapter 1.1, and the impulse response symbol h(t) or h[n] from Chapter 1.3.

blocks.text: Write the system as y = T{x}, where T is the operator, x is the input signal and y is the output signal. The system is linear when two inputs together give two outputs together, with constants kept outside.
T{a x₁ + b x₂} = a T{x₁} + b T{x₂}
blocks.where: x₁ and x₂ are any two input signals; a and b are any constants (real or complex); T{x₁} and T{x₂} are the outputs for those inputs.

blocks.text: The formula packs two rules. Set a = b = 1 to get additivity: T{x₁ + x₂} = T{x₁} + T{x₂}. Set b = 0 to get scaling (homogeneity): T{a x₁} = a T{x₁}. A system must pass both to be linear.

Linearity exists so that a complicated input can be split into simple pieces, each piece pushed through the system, and the outputs added. The impulse, step and exponential of Chapter 1.3 are exactly such pieces.

A quick test: a linear system must give zero output for zero input, because T{0} = T{0·x} = 0·T{x} = 0. So y(t) = x(t) + 2 is not linear, while y(t) = t x(t) is linear even though its coefficient changes with time.
Time invariance is about shifts, not about the system ageing. Delay the input by t₀ seconds and the whole output must delay by the same t₀, unchanged in shape.
x(t − t₀) → y(t − t₀)   for every t₀;   x[n − n₀] → y[n − n₀] for every integer n₀
blocks.where: t₀ is the delay in seconds for continuous time (CT); n₀ is the delay in samples for discrete time (DT); y is the output produced by x.

items: Take a test input x and find the output y = T{x}.
Form the shifted input x(t − t₀) and compute T{x(t − t₀)}.
Shift the original output to get y(t − t₀).
Compare the two results symbolically. Equal for all t₀ means time-invariant; one t₀ with unequal results is a counterexample.

blocks.text: Causality: the output at a chosen instant t₀ may depend only on input values at times t ≤ t₀, never on future input. A system that needs the next 5 ms of input is non-causal. Live systems such as a phone call or a motor controller must be causal. Recorded-data work, such as smoothing a stored ECG file, is allowed to be non-causal.

For an LTI system, causality and BIBO stability both reduce to tests on the impulse response h(t). Causality holds if and only if h(t) = 0 for t < 0 (h[n] = 0 for n < 0 in DT); the stability test comes in Section 3. Convolution and these LTI tests are developed under Causality and BIBO stability of LTI systems.
BIBO means bounded-input bounded-output. The system is BIBO stable when every input that never exceeds some finite size produces an output that also never exceeds some finite size.
if |x(t)| ≤ Mᵢₙ for all t, then |y(t)| ≤ Mₒᵤₜ for all t
blocks.where: Mᵢₙ is a finite bound on the input magnitude; Mₒᵤₜ is a finite bound on the output magnitude; the same statement with n in place of t covers DT.

blocks.text: For an LTI system the test moves onto h alone.

The absolute value matters. A bounded input can be shaped to match the sign of h at every instant, so the output can reach the full sum of magnitudes. If that sum is infinite, one bounded input drives the output to infinity. Example: h(t) = u(t) (a pure integrator) is causal but not stable, since ∫|h(t)|dt over all time is infinite.
The four tests are independent. A system can be linear and unstable, causal and time-varying, or stable and non-causal. Answer them one by one.

examples.question: A CT system is defined by y(t) = t x(t), with t in seconds and y in volt-seconds when x is in volts. Test it for linearity, time invariance, causality and BIBO stability. Use x(t) = 2 V as the bounded test input and the delay t₀ = 1 s.
steps: Linearity: T{a x₁ + b x₂} = t(a x₁ + b x₂) = a·t x₁ + b·t x₂ = a T{x₁} + b T{x₂}. Both additivity and scaling hold, so the system is linear.

Time invariance: the input x(t − 1) gives the output t x(t − 1). The shifted original output is (t − 1) x(t − 1). Take x = 2 V and t = 2 s. First result: 2 × 2 = 4 V·s. Second result: (2 − 1) × 2 = 2 V·s. They differ, so the system is time-varying.
Causality: the output at instant t uses x(t) at that same instant only, never a future value. The system is causal.

Stability: take the bounded input x(t) = 2 V, so Mᵢₙ = 2 V. Then y(t) = 2t V·s. At t = 10 s, |y| = 20 V·s. As t → ∞ the output grows without limit, so no finite Mₒᵤₜ exists. The system is not BIBO stable.
examples.answer: The system y(t) = t x(t) is linear, time-varying, causal and not BIBO stable.
examples.check:
M = 2.0
t = 2.0
t0 = 1.0
print(t * M)
print((t - t0) * M)
t2 = 10.0
print(t2 * M)

traps: Time invariance does not mean the system never changes with time. It means a shift in the input produces exactly that shift in the output. The coefficient t in t x(t) makes the system time-varying.
A constant added term breaks linearity. For y(t) = x(t) + 2, the zero input gives 2, not 0, so the superposition formula fails no matter how small the constant is.

Both linearity conditions are needed. Check scaling and additivity separately, because a system that fails either one is not linear. Example: y(t) = x²(t) fails scaling (T{a x} = a²x², not a x²) and fails additivity ((x₁ + x₂)² ≠ x₁² + x₂²).
Causality is about which input samples are used, not about how fast the output appears. A system using x(t + 1) is non-causal even if its output is delayed by an hour.
For LTI stability, take the absolute value inside the integral or sum. ∫h(t)dt finite does not guarantee stability; ∫|h(t)|dt must be finite.

quiz.q: State the two conditions inside the linearity definition.
quiz.a: Additivity, T{x₁ + x₂} = T{x₁} + T{x₂}, and scaling (homogeneity), T{a x} = a T{x} for any constant a.

quiz.q: Why does a linear system give zero output for zero input?
quiz.a: Set a = 0 in the scaling rule: T{0·x} = 0·T{x} = 0. So T{0} = 0, and any system with a nonzero zero-input output is not linear.

quiz.q: Test y[n] = x[2n] for time invariance. Use a counterexample with n₀ = 1.
quiz.a: Shifted input x[n − 1] gives x[2n − 1]. The shifted output is y[n − 1] = x[2(n − 1)] = x[2n − 2]. At n = 1 these are x[1] and x[0], which differ in general, so the system is time-varying. It is a decimator: it uses every second sample.

quiz.q: An LTI system has h(t) = e<sup>−2t</sup> u(t). Test it for causality and BIBO stability. Take the CT forms.
quiz.a: Causality: h(t) = 0 for t < 0 because of u(t), so it is causal. Stability: ∫₀<sup>∞</sup> e<sup>−2t</sup> dt = 1/2 = 0.5, which is finite, so the system is BIBO stable.

quiz.q: A system is causal and BIBO stable but not linear. Can it still be time-invariant? Give a one-line reason with an example.
quiz.a: Yes. The four properties are independent. Example: y(t) = |x(t)| is causal (uses only present input), stable (|y| = |x| ≤ Mᵢₙ), time-invariant (a shift in x gives the same shift in |x|), but not linear, since |x₁ + x₂| is not always |x₁| + |x₂|.

quiz.q: Why does the stability test for an LTI system use ∫|h(t)|dt rather than ∫h(t)dt?
quiz.a: A bounded input can be chosen to match the sign of h(t) at every instant, so every part of h adds with the same sign and the output can reach the full sum of magnitudes. If ∫|h(t)|dt is infinite, that bounded input produces an unbounded output. A finite ∫h(t)dt can still occur with signs cancelling, so it does not prove stability.

quiz.q: Give one practical situation where a non-causal system is acceptable.
quiz.a: Offline processing of a stored recording, such as smoothing a saved ECG or sharpening a photograph. The whole file is already available, so using future samples costs nothing and no real-time decision is delayed.

beyond: Not for the exam. The four tests are the gate to the LTI toolbox: once a system is linear and time-invariant, convolution with h(t) describes it completely, and the Laplace and Z transforms turn it into algebra on poles and zeros. Stability tests then become region-of-convergence checks on the Laplace and Z transforms instead of integrals. In control and communications practice, engineers also measure gain margin and phase margin, and for nonlinear blocks they linearise around an operating point before applying these tests. Search for BIBO stability, impulse response absolute summability, and bounded-input bounded-output in control texts to go further.
